name: Speed Import
description: The shortest path from a live website to a live Fluid storefront: brand, catalog, and source capture open together so the theme starts building in the second wave, then home, shop, product, publish. One model — Grok 4.5 — end to end; the only QA turn is the publish gate, which reworks a dead storefront but still cannot stop the run. Deliberately skips the onboarding form, content and collection import, media and UGC, and storefront QA; the handoff says so explicitly. Use Streamlined Onboard & Launch when the company needs to actually launch.

steps.name: Map the source catalog
steps.prompt:
Build the product source manifest. Call run_skill("fluid-product-admin-import") and follow its catalog completion contract. Read-only against Fluid.

WRITE AS YOU GO. Your context window is the binding constraint: fetching every product page and holding it in the conversation blows the model's prompt limit, which is a hard turn error that kills this step and everything downstream. Measured on a real catalog: 779,638 tokens against a 500,000 limit.

Discover identities first and append them to a JSONL manifest as you find them. Then enrich in batches of at most 20 — fetch, extract, append, drop the page. Never keep a fetched body in context after its fields are out, and never summarize batches back into the conversation. Prefer a products JSON endpoint or JSON-LD over a full page; when you must fetch a page, ask for markdown, not html.

Discovery is a union of sitemap, any structured catalog API, and every collection pagination followed to its end. Speed matters here, completeness matters more: a product you never discovered is a product the store cannot sell.

If room runs short, stop enriching and keep every discovered identity. A complete identity list with partial fields is recoverable; a dead step is not.

End with STEP_OUTPUT: { manifest_path, products, enriched, identity_only, variants, collections, unresolved: [...] }.

steps.name: Capture the source site
steps.prompt:
Capture the source home page once so the page steps build from evidence rather than re-crawling. Call run_skill("themes/theme-source-inventory") and follow it.

Home in full at desktop and at 390 wide, formats ["html", "rawHtml", "screenshot"], capturePageEvidence: true — that retains the site's own CSS labelled by origin and resolved computed styles for every text landmark. Plus a route inventory: the canonical URL for shop, one product, and the main content pages. Do not deep-capture every route.

Write clone-manifest.json with the route map and evidence paths.

End with STEP_OUTPUT: { routes: {...}, evidence: {...} }.

steps.name: Publish the theme
steps.prompt:
Publish the built theme.

1. Confirm no scaffold filler survived in the touched templates — placeholder names and starter-theme copy both count.
2. Record the development theme id and the release target id; they are not the same theme.
3. Push and activate the release target, then GET /api/application_themes/active and confirm the active id is the one you pushed.
4. Default-template audit (required). From the same GET /api/application_themes/active response, group the theme's templates by themeable_type and require a default:true entry for every type the storefront routes through: layouts, home_page, navbar, footer, product, collection, category, page, post, cart_page, shop_page, locales. A missing default:true template for a routed themeable_type is exactly what makes a live route render as HTTP 204 with an empty body. A theme MAY legitimately lack one of these types only if a working reference theme (one whose live routes render) shows the same gap. If a default is missing, fix it — mark the right template default:true or create it — and re-run this audit until it passes; do not report the gap and move on.
5. Load the live home URL and one product route in the browser and record, for each route, the HTTP status AND the response body byte count. Every checked route must return 200 with a non-empty rendered body and must not redirect to home. A 204, or any empty body, IS a failed publish — the theme is not live no matter what the activation API said. "The storefront QA step will catch it" is not an excuse to pass this step; fix the cause (almost always a missing default template from the audit above) and re-verify until every route returns 200 with a real body.
6. Confirm the header logo and any brand imagery in the templates resolve to Fluid DAM URLs, not the source site's CDN. The theme track builds from the source and does not wait on the brand step, so a source-CDN logo can survive into the templates; those links rot and leak the source domain. Repoint any that slipped through to the DAM URL the brand step persisted.


Publish even if a page step left findings; carry them into your output.

End with STEP_OUTPUT: { release_theme_id, active_theme_id, live_url, default_template_audit: {types_verified: [...], types_fixed: [...]}, routes_checked: [{route, status, body_bytes}], carried_findings: [...] }.
acceptance: The active application theme id equals the theme this run built and pushed.

The active theme has a default:true template for every routed themeable_type (layouts, home_page, navbar, footer, product, collection, category, page, post, cart_page, shop_page, locales), or a working reference theme demonstrably lacks the same type.

The live home route and at least one product route were checked with recorded HTTP status and body byte count per route, and every checked route returned 200 with a non-empty body — a 204 or empty body fails this step.
No template references the source site's CDN for the logo or brand imagery; those assets resolve to Fluid DAM URLs.

steps.name: What landed, and what needs you
steps.prompt:
Write the handoff. Pull each step's STEP_OUTPUT; re-do nothing.

Lead with the live storefront URL and one honest sentence on whether this company could take an order today. Then: what is live, with counts; what is blocking, each with the single action that clears it; and what this run deliberately skipped — business profile and onboarding form, collections and content pages, media and UGC, and any broad storefront QA. Those are not failures, they are the trade this workflow makes for speed, and the operator needs to know they are outstanding.

Counts, routes, and ids — not adjectives.

End with STEP_OUTPUT: { live_url, can_take_an_order: true|false, live: {...}, blocking: [...], not_attempted: [...] }.
